snapshots.name: Socrates
snapshots.body: The Athenian philosopher, invoked throughout as the standard of a life well lived: his equanimity in the face of death (Book 3), a sustained inquiry into what actually made him admirable rather than merely famous (Book 7), and a cluster of anecdotes about his poverty, his wife Xanthippe, and his refusal to fetch an innocent man for the Thirty Tyrants (Book 11).
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Antoninus Pius
snapshots.body: Marcus's adoptive father and predecessor as emperor. Book 6 gives him the work's longest sustained character portrait -- his patience, freedom from vanity, thoroughness, and equanimity under criticism -- held up as the standard Marcus measures himself against elsewhere (Books 4, 8, 10). Marcus was born Marcus Annius Verus and took the name Antoninus on adoption; a handful of bare "Antoninus" mentions elsewhere in the text are Marcus referring to himself, not to his father, and are not bound to this entry.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Verus (Marcus’s grandfather)
snapshots.body: Marcus's paternal grandfather, credited in the book's opening line with teaching him gentleness and freedom from anger. A second, unrelated "Verus" is Marcus's father, named later in Book 8.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Diognetus
snapshots.body: A teacher credited with turning young Marcus away from superstition and showmen's tricks and toward philosophy, and with introducing him to Bacchius, Tandasis, and Marcianus.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Junius Rusticus
snapshots.body: The teacher Marcus credits with first convincing him his life needed correction, with steering him away from showy rhetoric and toward plain writing, and with giving him his own copy of Epictetus's discourses.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Apollonius
snapshots.body: A Stoic teacher praised for combining unshakeable steadiness with warmth, and for taking favors from friends without becoming beholden to them.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Sextus
snapshots.body: A teacher praised for running his household with paternal warmth and for combining Stoic even-temperedness with genuine tenderness.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Alexander the Grammarian
snapshots.body: A grammar teacher credited with correcting others' language tactfully -- by supplying the right word in reply, never by pointing out the mistake directly. Not to be confused with Alexander the Platonist (also thanked in Book 1) or with Alexander the Great, named elsewhere in the book.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Fronto
snapshots.body: A teacher credited with warning Marcus how much envy, fraud, and hypocrisy attend absolute power, and how little natural affection the highborn often have.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Alexander the Platonist
snapshots.body: A Platonist teacher credited with teaching Marcus not to plead "I have no time" to friends who needed him. Not to be confused with Alexander the Grammarian (also thanked in Book 1) or with Alexander the Great, named elsewhere in the book.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Catulus
snapshots.body: A teacher credited with teaching Marcus not to dismiss a friend's complaint even when unfair, and to speak well of his own teachers, as he had heard was the practice of Domitius and Athenodotus.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Severus
snapshots.body: Marcus's "brother" (an honorific, not a blood relation) credited with introducing him to the examples of Thrasea, Helvidius, Cato, Dio, and Brutus, and with kindling his early ideal of a commonwealth governed by equal law. A second, unrelated bare "Severus" appears once more in Book 10's private list of namesakes (10:29); nothing there ties it back to this figure, so that occurrence is left unbound rather than assumed to be the same man.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Claudius Maximus
snapshots.body: A Stoic teacher praised for self-command, cheerfulness under hardship, and a manner so consistently upright that no one who knew him ever felt looked down on. A second, unrelated "Maximus" -- clearly a household figure, not this revered teacher -- appears once in Book 8's list of paired deaths (8:23).
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Bacchius
snapshots.body: One of the teachers Diognetus first brought Marcus to hear.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Tandasis
snapshots.body: One of the teachers Diognetus first brought Marcus to hear, named alongside Marcianus.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Marcianus
snapshots.body: One of the teachers Diognetus first brought Marcus to hear, named alongside Tandasis.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Domitius
snapshots.body: Cited, alongside Athenodotus, as an example of someone who spoke well of his own teachers on every occasion -- the practice Catulus taught Marcus to imitate.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Athenodotus
snapshots.body: Cited, alongside Domitius, as an example of someone who spoke well of his own teachers on every occasion -- the practice Catulus taught Marcus to imitate.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Thrasea
snapshots.body: Thrasea Paetus, the Roman senator executed under Nero for his principled opposition to imperial tyranny -- one of the exemplars of libertas that Severus introduced Marcus to.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Helvidius
snapshots.body: Helvidius Priscus, the Roman senator and Stoic executed under Vespasian for defying imperial authority -- one of the exemplars of libertas that Severus introduced Marcus to.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Dio
snapshots.body: Traditionally identified as Dio of Syracuse, the associate of Plato who tried to install philosophical rule there -- one of the exemplars of libertas that Severus introduced Marcus to, named alongside Brutus and Cato.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Brutus
snapshots.body: Marcus Junius Brutus, leader of the conspiracy against Julius Caesar -- one of the exemplars of libertas that Severus introduced Marcus to.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Cato
snapshots.body: Cato the Younger, the Stoic senator and fierce opponent of Julius Caesar who became the standard Roman symbol of principled resistance to tyranny -- one of the exemplars of libertas that Severus introduced Marcus to (1:10), named alongside Thrasea, Helvidius, Dio, and Brutus. A second, unrelated bare "Cato" appears in Book 4's undifferentiated list of forgotten Roman names (4:27, alongside an equally unbound "Scipio"); nothing there distinguishes which Cato is meant, so that occurrence is left unbound rather than assumed to be this same man.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Benedicta
snapshots.body: Named as a woman Marcus reports he never had any involvement with, in a passage thanking the gods for the restraint of his youth.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Theodotus
snapshots.body: Named alongside Benedicta as someone Marcus reports he never had any involvement with, in a passage thanking the gods for the restraint of his youth.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Chryses
snapshots.body: The priest of Apollo from the opening of Homer's Iliad, who prays for his daughter's return on the seashore and is answered. Marcus cites him as a precedent for a dream that once resolved a physical complaint of his own.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Hippocrates
snapshots.body: The celebrated Greek physician, cited as proof that even a healer of many is not spared his own death.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Pompey
snapshots.body: Pompey the Great, the Roman general, cited twice as an example of a great conqueror who nonetheless had to die like anyone else, grouped both times with Alexander and Julius Caesar.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Julius Caesar
snapshots.body: Named "Caius Caesar" (and, once, bare "Caius"), cited twice as an example of a great conqueror who nonetheless had to die like anyone else, grouped both times with Alexander and Pompey.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Heraclitus
snapshots.body: The philosopher of universal flux and periodic world-conflagration, cited repeatedly (Books 3, 4, 6) both for his death -- from dropsy, an irony given his own theories about fire and water -- and for his teaching that even sleepers contribute to the world's workings.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Democritus
snapshots.body: The atomist philosopher, cited as proof that even a great mind is not spared an undignified death -- killed, Marcus says, by lice.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Phalaris
snapshots.body: The tyrant of Acragas, proverbial in antiquity for cruelty, cited as an example of the intolerable use of power alongside Nero.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Nero
snapshots.body: The Roman emperor notorious for tyranny, cited alongside Phalaris as an example of the intolerable use of power.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Cadicianus
snapshots.body: An otherwise unidentified name in a list of once-familiar Romans now forgotten, alongside Fabius, Julianus, and Lepidus. Original-en prints "Cadiciant's," a Gutenberg transcription slip for "Cadicianus's"; both spellings are aliased and the slip is left as printed, not corrected.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Fabius (Book 4)
snapshots.body: An otherwise unidentified name in a list of once-familiar Romans now forgotten, alongside Cadicianus, Julianus, and Lepidus. A different, fully named "Fabius Catulinus" appears later, in Book 12's separate list.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Julianus
snapshots.body: An otherwise unidentified name in a list of once-familiar Romans now forgotten, alongside Cadicianus, Fabius, and Lepidus.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Lepidus
snapshots.body: An otherwise unidentified name in a list of once-familiar Romans now forgotten, alongside Cadicianus, Fabius, and Julianus.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Camillus
snapshots.body: Marcus Furius Camillus, the early Roman general and statesman sometimes called Rome's "second founder," cited as the first name in a chronological list of once-famous Romans now fading into obscurity.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Caeso
snapshots.body: An early, semi-legendary Roman name in the same list of once-famous Romans now forgotten, alongside Volesius and Leonnatus.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Volesius
snapshots.body: An early, semi-legendary Roman name in the same list of once-famous Romans now forgotten, alongside Caeso and Leonnatus.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Leonnatus
snapshots.body: One of Alexander the Great's Macedonian generals, cited in the same list of once-famous names now forgotten, alongside Caeso and Volesius.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Augustus
snapshots.body: Rome's first emperor, cited repeatedly as an example of a once supremely powerful figure now reduced to a name in a list -- his whole court (Book 8) and household (Book 8) are cited as an example of the death of an entire retinue.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Agathon
snapshots.body: The Athenian tragic poet, a character in Plato's Symposium. Marcus quotes a saying attributed to him about minding one's own conduct rather than others' faults.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Cecrops
snapshots.body: The legendary founding king of Athens. Marcus quotes an unnamed saying, "beloved city of Cecrops," as a model for how he ought to address the world itself.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Vespasian
snapshots.body: The Roman emperor, cited as an example of a bygone age whose people did all the same ordinary things people do now -- marrying, quarreling, dying -- and are now entirely gone.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Trajan
snapshots.body: The Roman emperor, cited alongside Vespasian as an example of a bygone age now entirely gone.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Alexander the Great
snapshots.body: The Macedonian conqueror, cited repeatedly (Books 3, 6, 8, 9, 10) as the paradigm case of a life of vast worldly power that ends, like any other, in death -- once compared directly to the mule driver who died alongside him.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Crates
snapshots.body: The Cynic philosopher, cited for a (lost) remark about Xenocrates.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Xenocrates
snapshots.body: The philosopher and head of Plato's Academy, the subject of a (lost) remark by Crates that Marcus tells the reader to look up.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Aesculapius
snapshots.body: The god of healing and medicine. Marcus asks rhetorically whether Aesculapius oversteps his own function the way a person might overstep theirs.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Chrysippus
snapshots.body: The Stoic philosopher and systematizer of the school, cited twice (Books 6, 7) -- once for a joke he made about a bad line being part of a larger comedy.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Philistio
snapshots.body: An otherwise unidentified name among a catalog of the dead of every profession, alongside Phoebus and Origanion.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Phoebus
snapshots.body: An otherwise unidentified name among a catalog of the dead of every profession, alongside Philistio and Origanion -- likely an ordinary person bearing the god Apollo's epithet as a name, not the god himself.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Origanion
snapshots.body: An otherwise unidentified name among a catalog of the dead of every profession, alongside Philistio and Phoebus.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Eudoxus
snapshots.body: The Greek astronomer and mathematician, cited in a catalog of great minds now dead, alongside Hipparchus and Archimedes.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Hipparchus
snapshots.body: The Greek astronomer, cited in the same catalog of great minds now dead, alongside Eudoxus and Archimedes.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Archimedes
snapshots.body: The Greek mathematician and engineer, cited in the same catalog of great minds now dead, alongside Eudoxus and Hipparchus.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Menippus
snapshots.body: The Cynic satirist, cited as an example of those who mocked the brevity and fragility of human life, and who are themselves now just as dead as everyone else.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Antisthenes
snapshots.body: The Cynic philosopher and associate of Socrates, cited for a one-line saying about the cost of good and bad deeds becoming known.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Leon of Salamis
snapshots.body: The Athenian whom the Thirty Tyrants ordered Socrates to arrest; Socrates's refusal, at personal risk, is cited as one of the acts that made him admirable. Named here by the epithet "Salaminius," the Salaminian.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Plato
snapshots.body: The philosopher, cited repeatedly (Books 7, 9, 10, 11) as an authority -- his view that no soul errs willingly, his ideal "commonwealth" used as a byword for an unrealistic political hope, and, alongside Hesiod, as a source for the myth of the Isles of the Blessed.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Epicurus
snapshots.body: The philosopher of atomism and pleasure, cited repeatedly (Books 7, 9, 10) as the representative of the view Marcus argues against -- that the world is mere accidental atoms rather than governed by providence -- though Marcus notes that even on Epicurus's own terms his conclusions about death still hold.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Africanus
snapshots.body: Scipio Africanus, the Roman general who defeated Hannibal, cited alongside Augustus as proof that no man, however famous, is remembered forever.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Faustina
snapshots.body: Faustina the Elder, wife of Antoninus Pius, cited in Book 8's list of paired deaths: she predeceased her husband, who himself died afterward.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Hadrian
snapshots.body: The Roman emperor and Antoninus Pius's predecessor, cited repeatedly (Books 4, 8, 10) as an example of a once-supreme figure now merely a name -- his whole court, his household attendants, and his own death are each cited in turn.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Celer
snapshots.body: Named first in a chain of paired deaths in Hadrian's circle -- "first Celer, [then] Hadrian; then Hadrian himself" -- suggesting Celer predeceased the emperor he served.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Charax
snapshots.body: One of the once-"austere" figures Marcus lists as now dead and mostly forgotten, alongside Demetrius the Platonic and Eudaemon.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Demetrius the Platonic
snapshots.body: One of the once-"austere" figures Marcus lists as now dead and mostly forgotten, alongside Charax and Eudaemon. A different, fully named "Demetrius Phalereus" appears later, in Book 9.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Eudaemon
snapshots.body: One of the once-"austere" figures Marcus lists as now dead and mostly forgotten, alongside Charax and Demetrius the Platonic.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Secunda
snapshots.body: Named in Book 8's list of paired deaths -- "Secunda, Maximus; then Secunda herself" -- suggesting she outlived a household figure named Maximus before dying in turn.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Maximus (Book 8)
snapshots.body: An unidentified household figure named in Book 8's list of paired deaths, alongside Secunda -- not the revered Stoic teacher Claudius Maximus of Book 1, given the company he keeps here (Epitynchanus, Diotimus, Celer, Charax, Eudaemon).
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Epitynchanus
snapshots.body: Named in Book 8's list of paired deaths -- "Epitynchanus, Diotimus; then Epitynchanus himself" -- suggesting he outlived Diotimus before dying in turn.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Diotimus
snapshots.body: Named twice in Book 8 as a companion of the powerful now dead: paired with Epitynchanus in the list of successive deaths (8:23), and named again, alongside Chabrias, as one of Hadrian's attendants who lingered by his tomb (8:34).
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Lucilla
snapshots.body: Traditionally identified as Domitia Lucilla, Marcus's mother. Opens Book 8's list of paired deaths: "Lucilla buried Verus; then was Lucilla herself buried by others" -- read as Marcus's mother outliving his father before dying in turn.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Verus (Marcus’s father)
snapshots.body: Traditionally identified as Marcus's own father, who died when Marcus was a small child, in the couplet "Lucilla buried Verus; then was Lucilla herself buried by others" (8:23) -- read as Marcus's mother outliving his father before dying in turn. A second, unrelated "Verus" is Marcus's paternal grandfather, named in the book's opening line.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Senate
snapshots.body: The Roman Senate, cited among the institutions Augustus is recorded as having carefully managed.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Agrippa
snapshots.body: Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa, Augustus's general and son-in-law, cited as part of the entire vanished court of Augustus.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Areus
snapshots.body: Arius Didymus, the philosopher and close friend of Augustus, cited as part of the entire vanished court of Augustus.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Maecenas
snapshots.body: Gaius Maecenas, Augustus's celebrated patron and advisor, cited as part of the entire vanished court of Augustus.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Pompeys
snapshots.body: The family of Pompey the Great, cited as an example of an entire once-powerful lineage that eventually runs out, quoting an epitaph: "He was the last of his own kindred."
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Panthea
snapshots.body: Named, alongside Pergamus, as an attendant who supposedly lingered by a master's tomb -- cited by Marcus as a foolish example of misplaced devotion to the dead.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Pergamus
snapshots.body: Named, alongside Panthea, as an attendant who supposedly lingered by a master's tomb -- cited by Marcus as a foolish example of misplaced devotion to the dead.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Chabrias
snapshots.body: Named, alongside Diotimus, as one of Hadrian's attendants who supposedly lingered by the emperor's tomb -- cited by Marcus as a foolish example of misplaced devotion to the dead.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Demetrius Phalereus
snapshots.body: Demetrius of Phalerum, the Athenian statesman and philosopher who governed Athens under Macedonian oversight, cited alongside Alexander and Philip as an example of political men whose self-command Marcus refuses to imitate. A different, otherwise unidentified "Demetrius the Platonic" appears earlier, in Book 8.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Philip of Macedon
snapshots.body: Alexander the Great's father, cited twice (Books 9, 10) alongside Alexander as an example of a once-supreme ruler whose entire court is now merely a name in a list.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Hesiod
snapshots.body: The early Greek poet, cited alongside Plato as a source for the myth of the Isles of the Blessed (the Elysian Fields).
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Croesus
snapshots.body: The legendarily wealthy king of Lydia, cited alongside Hadrian, Antoninus Pius, Philip, and Alexander as an example of a once-supreme figure whose entire court is now merely a name in a list.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Satyro
snapshots.body: An unidentified contemporary of Marcus's, the first in a private list of paired names (10:29) whose exact point of comparison -- to Socraticus and Eutyches, or Hymen -- is not recoverable from the text.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Socraticus
snapshots.body: An unidentified figure paired with Satyro in Marcus's private list of comparisons (10:29), alongside Eutyches or Hymen.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Eutyches
snapshots.body: An unidentified figure paired with Satyro in Marcus's private list of comparisons (10:29), alongside Socraticus or Hymen.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Hymen
snapshots.body: An unidentified figure paired with Satyro in Marcus's private list of comparisons (10:29) -- likely a person bearing the name of the Greek marriage-god as a personal name, rather than the god himself.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Euphrates
snapshots.body: Possibly Euphrates of Tyre, a Stoic philosopher of Marcus's own era praised by other contemporary writers, though the text gives no detail beyond the bare name in this private list of comparisons (10:29), paired with Eutychio and Sylvanus.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Eutychio
snapshots.body: An unidentified figure paired with Euphrates in Marcus's private list of comparisons (10:29), alongside Sylvanus.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Sylvanus
snapshots.body: An unidentified figure paired with Euphrates in Marcus's private list of comparisons (10:29), alongside Eutychio.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Alciphron
snapshots.body: An unidentified figure in Marcus's private list of comparisons (10:29), paired with Tropaeophorus.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Tropaeophorus
snapshots.body: An unidentified figure paired with Alciphron in Marcus's private list of comparisons (10:29).
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Xenophon
snapshots.body: The Athenian historian and associate of Socrates, cited as one half of the closing pair in Marcus's private list of comparisons (10:29), alongside Crito or Severus.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Crito
snapshots.body: Socrates's friend, present at his death in Plato's dialogues, cited as one of the figures Xenophon is compared to in Marcus's private list of comparisons (10:29).
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Empedocles
snapshots.body: The philosopher whose image of the soul as a perfect, self-sufficient sphere Marcus borrows twice (Books 11, 12) as a model for the ideal disposition of the mind.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Phocion
snapshots.body: The Athenian statesman noted for showing his critics their errors gently rather than scornfully -- cited as a model for how to respond to those who hate or contemn you, so long as the anecdote isn't exaggerated.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Diogenes
snapshots.body: The Cynic philosopher, cited twice (Books 8, 11) as an example of genuine philosophical seriousness -- once for having earned, through his own directness, the liberty later claimed by Old Comedy.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Hercules
snapshots.body: The mythical hero, invoked as "the guide and leader of the Muses" as the source of a tenth maxim about not resenting that wicked people exist.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Perdiccas
snapshots.body: Traditionally identified as Perdiccas II, king of Macedon and a contemporary of Socrates, said to have invited Socrates to his court -- an invitation Socrates is quoted here as having declined.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Xanthippe
snapshots.body: Socrates's wife, named in an anecdote about Socrates good-naturedly wearing an animal skin after she took his clothes away.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Fabius Catulinus
snapshots.body: An otherwise unidentified Roman named in Book 12's list of vanished examples of "vehement prosecution in worldly matters," alongside Lucius Lupus, Stertinius, Tiberius, and Velius Rufus. A different, unrelated bare "Fabius" appears earlier, in Book 4's separate list.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Lucius Lupus
snapshots.body: An otherwise unidentified Roman named in the same Book 12 list, alongside Fabius Catulinus, Stertinius, Tiberius, and Velius Rufus.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Stertinius
snapshots.body: An otherwise unidentified Roman named in the same Book 12 list, alongside Fabius Catulinus, Lucius Lupus, Tiberius, and Velius Rufus.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Tiberius
snapshots.body: The Roman emperor who spent his final years in seclusion at Capreae (Capri), named in the same Book 12 list as an example of "vehement prosecution in worldly matters" now vanished.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Velius Rufus
snapshots.body: An otherwise unidentified Roman named in the same Book 12 list, alongside Fabius Catulinus, Lucius Lupus, and Stertinius.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Socrates
snapshots.body: The Athenian philosopher, invoked throughout as the standard of a life well lived: his equanimity in the face of death (Book 3), a sustained inquiry into what actually made him admirable rather than merely famous (Book 7), and a cluster of anecdotes about his poverty, his wife Xanthippe, and his refusal to fetch an innocent man for the Thirty Tyrants (Book 11).
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Antoninus Pius
snapshots.body: Marcus's adoptive father and predecessor as emperor. Book 6 gives him the work's longest sustained character portrait -- his patience, freedom from vanity, thoroughness, and equanimity under criticism -- held up as the standard Marcus measures himself against elsewhere (Books 4, 8, 10). Marcus was born Marcus Annius Verus and took the name Antoninus on adoption; a handful of bare "Antoninus" mentions elsewhere in the text are Marcus referring to himself, not to his father, and are not bound to this entry.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Verus (Marcus’s grandfather)
snapshots.body: Marcus's paternal grandfather, credited in the book's opening line with teaching him gentleness and freedom from anger. A second, unrelated "Verus" is Marcus's father, named later in Book 8.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Diognetus
snapshots.body: A teacher credited with turning young Marcus away from superstition and showmen's tricks and toward philosophy, and with introducing him to Bacchius, Tandasis, and Marcianus.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Junius Rusticus
snapshots.body: The teacher Marcus credits with first convincing him his life needed correction, with steering him away from showy rhetoric and toward plain writing, and with giving him his own copy of Epictetus's discourses.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Apollonius
snapshots.body: A Stoic teacher praised for combining unshakeable steadiness with warmth, and for taking favors from friends without becoming beholden to them.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Sextus
snapshots.body: A teacher praised for running his household with paternal warmth and for combining Stoic even-temperedness with genuine tenderness.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Alexander the Grammarian
snapshots.body: A grammar teacher credited with correcting others' language tactfully -- by supplying the right word in reply, never by pointing out the mistake directly. Not to be confused with Alexander the Platonist (also thanked in Book 1) or with Alexander the Great, named elsewhere in the book.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Fronto
snapshots.body: A teacher credited with warning Marcus how much envy, fraud, and hypocrisy attend absolute power, and how little natural affection the highborn often have.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Alexander the Platonist
snapshots.body: A Platonist teacher credited with teaching Marcus not to plead "I have no time" to friends who needed him. Not to be confused with Alexander the Grammarian (also thanked in Book 1) or with Alexander the Great, named elsewhere in the book.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Catulus
snapshots.body: A teacher credited with teaching Marcus not to dismiss a friend's complaint even when unfair, and to speak well of his own teachers, as he had heard was the practice of Domitius and Athenodotus.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Severus
snapshots.body: Marcus's "brother" (an honorific, not a blood relation) credited with introducing him to the examples of Thrasea, Helvidius, Cato, Dio, and Brutus, and with kindling his early ideal of a commonwealth governed by equal law. A second, unrelated bare "Severus" appears once more in Book 10's private list of namesakes (10:29); nothing there ties it back to this figure, so that occurrence is left unbound rather than assumed to be the same man.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Claudius Maximus
snapshots.body: A Stoic teacher praised for self-command, cheerfulness under hardship, and a manner so consistently upright that no one who knew him ever felt looked down on. A second, unrelated "Maximus" -- clearly a household figure, not this revered teacher -- appears once in Book 8's list of paired deaths (8:23).
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Bacchius
snapshots.body: One of the teachers Diognetus first brought Marcus to hear.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Tandasis
snapshots.body: One of the teachers Diognetus first brought Marcus to hear, named alongside Marcianus.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Marcianus
snapshots.body: One of the teachers Diognetus first brought Marcus to hear, named alongside Tandasis.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Domitius
snapshots.body: Cited, alongside Athenodotus, as an example of someone who spoke well of his own teachers on every occasion -- the practice Catulus taught Marcus to imitate.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Athenodotus
snapshots.body: Cited, alongside Domitius, as an example of someone who spoke well of his own teachers on every occasion -- the practice Catulus taught Marcus to imitate.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Thrasea
snapshots.body: Thrasea Paetus, the Roman senator executed under Nero for his principled opposition to imperial tyranny -- one of the exemplars of libertas that Severus introduced Marcus to.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Helvidius
snapshots.body: Helvidius Priscus, the Roman senator and Stoic executed under Vespasian for defying imperial authority -- one of the exemplars of libertas that Severus introduced Marcus to.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Dio
snapshots.body: Traditionally identified as Dio of Syracuse, the associate of Plato who tried to install philosophical rule there -- one of the exemplars of libertas that Severus introduced Marcus to, named alongside Brutus and Cato.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Brutus
snapshots.body: Marcus Junius Brutus, leader of the conspiracy against Julius Caesar -- one of the exemplars of libertas that Severus introduced Marcus to.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Cato
snapshots.body: Cato the Younger, the Stoic senator and fierce opponent of Julius Caesar who became the standard Roman symbol of principled resistance to tyranny -- one of the exemplars of libertas that Severus introduced Marcus to (1:10), named alongside Thrasea, Helvidius, Dio, and Brutus. A second, unrelated bare "Cato" appears in Book 4's undifferentiated list of forgotten Roman names (4:27, alongside an equally unbound "Scipio"); nothing there distinguishes which Cato is meant, so that occurrence is left unbound rather than assumed to be this same man.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Benedicta
snapshots.body: Named as a woman Marcus reports he never had any involvement with, in a passage thanking the gods for the restraint of his youth.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Theodotus
snapshots.body: Named alongside Benedicta as someone Marcus reports he never had any involvement with, in a passage thanking the gods for the restraint of his youth.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Chryses
snapshots.body: The priest of Apollo from the opening of Homer's Iliad, who prays for his daughter's return on the seashore and is answered. Marcus cites him as a precedent for a dream that once resolved a physical complaint of his own.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Hippocrates
snapshots.body: The celebrated Greek physician, cited as proof that even a healer of many is not spared his own death.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Pompey
snapshots.body: Pompey the Great, the Roman general, cited twice as an example of a great conqueror who nonetheless had to die like anyone else, grouped both times with Alexander and Julius Caesar.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Julius Caesar
snapshots.body: Named "Caius Caesar" (and, once, bare "Caius"), cited twice as an example of a great conqueror who nonetheless had to die like anyone else, grouped both times with Alexander and Pompey.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Heraclitus
snapshots.body: The philosopher of universal flux and periodic world-conflagration, cited repeatedly (Books 3, 4, 6) both for his death -- from dropsy, an irony given his own theories about fire and water -- and for his teaching that even sleepers contribute to the world's workings.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Democritus
snapshots.body: The atomist philosopher, cited as proof that even a great mind is not spared an undignified death -- killed, Marcus says, by lice.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Phalaris
snapshots.body: The tyrant of Acragas, proverbial in antiquity for cruelty, cited as an example of the intolerable use of power alongside Nero.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Nero
snapshots.body: The Roman emperor notorious for tyranny, cited alongside Phalaris as an example of the intolerable use of power.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Cadicianus
snapshots.body: An otherwise unidentified name in a list of once-familiar Romans now forgotten, alongside Fabius, Julianus, and Lepidus. Original-en prints "Cadiciant's," a Gutenberg transcription slip for "Cadicianus's"; both spellings are aliased and the slip is left as printed, not corrected.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Fabius (Book 4)
snapshots.body: An otherwise unidentified name in a list of once-familiar Romans now forgotten, alongside Cadicianus, Julianus, and Lepidus. A different, fully named "Fabius Catulinus" appears later, in Book 12's separate list.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Julianus
snapshots.body: An otherwise unidentified name in a list of once-familiar Romans now forgotten, alongside Cadicianus, Fabius, and Lepidus.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Lepidus
snapshots.body: An otherwise unidentified name in a list of once-familiar Romans now forgotten, alongside Cadicianus, Fabius, and Julianus.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Camillus
snapshots.body: Marcus Furius Camillus, the early Roman general and statesman sometimes called Rome's "second founder," cited as the first name in a chronological list of once-famous Romans now fading into obscurity.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Caeso
snapshots.body: An early, semi-legendary Roman name in the same list of once-famous Romans now forgotten, alongside Volesius and Leonnatus.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Volesius
snapshots.body: An early, semi-legendary Roman name in the same list of once-famous Romans now forgotten, alongside Caeso and Leonnatus.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Leonnatus
snapshots.body: One of Alexander the Great's Macedonian generals, cited in the same list of once-famous names now forgotten, alongside Caeso and Volesius.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Augustus
snapshots.body: Rome's first emperor, cited repeatedly as an example of a once supremely powerful figure now reduced to a name in a list -- his whole court (Book 8) and household (Book 8) are cited as an example of the death of an entire retinue.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Agathon
snapshots.body: The Athenian tragic poet, a character in Plato's Symposium. Marcus quotes a saying attributed to him about minding one's own conduct rather than others' faults.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Cecrops
snapshots.body: The legendary founding king of Athens. Marcus quotes an unnamed saying, "beloved city of Cecrops," as a model for how he ought to address the world itself.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Vespasian
snapshots.body: The Roman emperor, cited as an example of a bygone age whose people did all the same ordinary things people do now -- marrying, quarreling, dying -- and are now entirely gone.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Trajan
snapshots.body: The Roman emperor, cited alongside Vespasian as an example of a bygone age now entirely gone.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Alexander the Great
snapshots.body: The Macedonian conqueror, cited repeatedly (Books 3, 6, 8, 9, 10) as the paradigm case of a life of vast worldly power that ends, like any other, in death -- once compared directly to the mule driver who died alongside him.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Crates
snapshots.body: The Cynic philosopher, cited for a (lost) remark about Xenocrates.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Xenocrates
snapshots.body: The philosopher and head of Plato's Academy, the subject of a (lost) remark by Crates that Marcus tells the reader to look up.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Aesculapius
snapshots.body: The god of healing and medicine. Marcus asks rhetorically whether Aesculapius oversteps his own function the way a person might overstep theirs.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Chrysippus
snapshots.body: The Stoic philosopher and systematizer of the school, cited twice (Books 6, 7) -- once for a joke he made about a bad line being part of a larger comedy.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Philistio
snapshots.body: An otherwise unidentified name among a catalog of the dead of every profession, alongside Phoebus and Origanion.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Phoebus
snapshots.body: An otherwise unidentified name among a catalog of the dead of every profession, alongside Philistio and Origanion -- likely an ordinary person bearing the god Apollo's epithet as a name, not the god himself.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Origanion
snapshots.body: An otherwise unidentified name among a catalog of the dead of every profession, alongside Philistio and Phoebus.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Eudoxus
snapshots.body: The Greek astronomer and mathematician, cited in a catalog of great minds now dead, alongside Hipparchus and Archimedes.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Hipparchus
snapshots.body: The Greek astronomer, cited in the same catalog of great minds now dead, alongside Eudoxus and Archimedes.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Archimedes
snapshots.body: The Greek mathematician and engineer, cited in the same catalog of great minds now dead, alongside Eudoxus and Hipparchus.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Menippus
snapshots.body: The Cynic satirist, cited as an example of those who mocked the brevity and fragility of human life, and who are themselves now just as dead as everyone else.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Antisthenes
snapshots.body: The Cynic philosopher and associate of Socrates, cited for a one-line saying about the cost of good and bad deeds becoming known.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Leon of Salamis
snapshots.body: The Athenian whom the Thirty Tyrants ordered Socrates to arrest; Socrates's refusal, at personal risk, is cited as one of the acts that made him admirable. Named here by the epithet "Salaminius," the Salaminian.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Plato
snapshots.body: The philosopher, cited repeatedly (Books 7, 9, 10, 11) as an authority -- his view that no soul errs willingly, his ideal "commonwealth" used as a byword for an unrealistic political hope, and, alongside Hesiod, as a source for the myth of the Isles of the Blessed.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Epicurus
snapshots.body: The philosopher of atomism and pleasure, cited repeatedly (Books 7, 9, 10) as the representative of the view Marcus argues against -- that the world is mere accidental atoms rather than governed by providence -- though Marcus notes that even on Epicurus's own terms his conclusions about death still hold.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Africanus
snapshots.body: Scipio Africanus, the Roman general who defeated Hannibal, cited alongside Augustus as proof that no man, however famous, is remembered forever.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Faustina
snapshots.body: Faustina the Elder, wife of Antoninus Pius, cited in Book 8's list of paired deaths: she predeceased her husband, who himself died afterward.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Hadrian
snapshots.body: The Roman emperor and Antoninus Pius's predecessor, cited repeatedly (Books 4, 8, 10) as an example of a once-supreme figure now merely a name -- his whole court, his household attendants, and his own death are each cited in turn.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Celer
snapshots.body: Named first in a chain of paired deaths in Hadrian's circle -- "first Celer, [then] Hadrian; then Hadrian himself" -- suggesting Celer predeceased the emperor he served.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Charax
snapshots.body: One of the once-"austere" figures Marcus lists as now dead and mostly forgotten, alongside Demetrius the Platonic and Eudaemon.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Demetrius the Platonic
snapshots.body: One of the once-"austere" figures Marcus lists as now dead and mostly forgotten, alongside Charax and Eudaemon. A different, fully named "Demetrius Phalereus" appears later, in Book 9.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Eudaemon
snapshots.body: One of the once-"austere" figures Marcus lists as now dead and mostly forgotten, alongside Charax and Demetrius the Platonic.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Secunda
snapshots.body: Named in Book 8's list of paired deaths -- "Secunda, Maximus; then Secunda herself" -- suggesting she outlived a household figure named Maximus before dying in turn.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Maximus (Book 8)
snapshots.body: An unidentified household figure named in Book 8's list of paired deaths, alongside Secunda -- not the revered Stoic teacher Claudius Maximus of Book 1, given the company he keeps here (Epitynchanus, Diotimus, Celer, Charax, Eudaemon).
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Epitynchanus
snapshots.body: Named in Book 8's list of paired deaths -- "Epitynchanus, Diotimus; then Epitynchanus himself" -- suggesting he outlived Diotimus before dying in turn.

snapshots.name: Diotimus
snapshots.body: Named twice in Book 8 as a companion of the powerful now dead: paired with Epitynchanus in the list of successive deaths (8:23), and named again, alongside Chabrias, as one of Hadrian's attendants who lingered by his tomb (8:34).

snapshots.name: Lucilla
snapshots.body: Traditionally identified as Domitia Lucilla, Marcus's mother. Opens Book 8's list of paired deaths: "Lucilla buried Verus; then was Lucilla herself buried by others" -- read as Marcus's mother outliving his father before dying in turn.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Verus (Marcus’s father)
snapshots.body: Traditionally identified as Marcus's own father, who died when Marcus was a small child, in the couplet "Lucilla buried Verus; then was Lucilla herself buried by others" (8:23) -- read as Marcus's mother outliving his father before dying in turn. A second, unrelated "Verus" is Marcus's paternal grandfather, named in the book's opening line.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Senate

snapshots.name: Agrippa

snapshots.name: The Pompeys
snapshots.body: The family of Pompey the Great, cited as an example of an entire once-powerful lineage that eventually runs out, quoting an epitaph: "He was the last of his own kindred."

snapshots.name: Panthea
snapshots.body: Named, alongside Pergamus, as an attendant who supposedly lingered by a master's tomb -- cited by Marcus as a foolish example of misplaced devotion to the dead.

snapshots.name: Demetrius Phalereus
snapshots.body: Demetrius of Phalerum, the Athenian statesman and philosopher who governed Athens under Macedonian oversight, cited alongside Alexander and Philip as an example of political men whose self-command Marcus refuses to imitate. A different, otherwise unidentified "Demetrius the Platonic" appears earlier, in Book 8.

snapshots.name: Philip of Macedon
snapshots.body: Alexander the Great's father, cited twice (Books 9, 10) alongside Alexander as an example of a once-supreme ruler whose entire court is now merely a name in a list.

snapshots.name: Hesiod

snapshots.name: Croesus

snapshots.name: Satyro

snapshots.name: Empedocles
snapshots.body: The philosopher whose image of the soul as a perfect, self-sufficient sphere Marcus borrows twice (Books 11, 12) as a model for the ideal disposition of the mind.

snapshots.name: Phocion
snapshots.body: The Athenian statesman noted for showing his critics their errors gently rather than scornfully -- cited as a model for how to respond to those who hate or contemn you, so long as the anecdote isn't exaggerated.

snapshots.name: Diogenes
snapshots.body: The Cynic philosopher, cited twice (Books 8, 11) as an example of genuine philosophical seriousness -- once for having earned, through his own directness, the liberty later claimed by Old Comedy.

snapshots.name: Hercules
snapshots.body: The mythical hero, invoked as "the guide and leader of the Muses" as the source of a tenth maxim about not resenting that wicked people exist.

snapshots.name: Perdiccas
snapshots.body: Traditionally identified as Perdiccas II, king of Macedon and a contemporary of Socrates, said to have invited Socrates to his court -- an invitation Socrates is quoted here as having declined.

snapshots.name: Xanthippe
snapshots.body: Socrates's wife, named in an anecdote about Socrates good-naturedly wearing an animal skin after she took his clothes away.
